parts: TEMPERAMENT

A sturdy dog with an abundant coat, a proud bearing and a chrysanthemum-like face. Intelligent, active and alert, with a friendly and independent temperament. As its name suggests, the Shih Tzu comes from Tibet, and its name means "lion dog". During the Manchu T´sing dynasty, it was considered a sacred dog, and numerous examples of this privileged animal lived in the imperial palace until the early 20th century. Proud and headstrong, it is a very playful dog, and it has been said that it "resembles a lion in appearance, a cat in its independent nature and a monkey in the faces it makes".

Its intelligence allows it to understand quickly and clearly what is expected of it, but its independence often leads it to respond indifferently to any command: it may assume an inscrutable air of "Eastern wisdom" before its owner, then proceed to do exactly as it pleases.

It is sociable with other dogs, treating them as equals even when they are ten times its size. Perhaps because of its small size, it gets along reasonably well with cats and can share a home with them in wonderful companionship. It gets on well with children and is amiable and friendly towards adults, even strangers.

If the Shih-Tzu's physical features perfectly evoke the East, the same can be said of its character: its personality is complex, elusive, enigmatic...; in other words, it has one of the most complex and unfathomable temperaments in the canine world. This is hardly surprising, as it spent centuries amid the intricacies of the secluded Chinese imperial court and alongside the inhabitants of the mysterious Himalayan monasteries. To explain this dog's many facets, it is said to have 'something of an icon', a little of the rabbit, the cat's suspicious nature, a touch of an elderly Chinese man, something of a monkey and a seal pup, the skin of a dancer and a hint of the bear in its coat. And the rest is pure Eastern mysticism.
STANDARD

The head is broad and round, with plenty of width between the eyes. The hair on the head should be tousled and fall well over the eyes. The beard and whiskers should be abundant. The hair on the nose should grow upwards, creating the characteristic chrysanthemum-like effect.
The muzzle should be broad, square, short, flat, well covered with hair and free from wrinkles.
The nose is black, although it may be dark liver in liver-coloured dogs or dogs with liver markings. The distance from the tip to the well-defined stop should be almost one inch (2,54 cm).

The muzzle is level or slightly upturned at the tip. The top of the nose should be level with or slightly below the lower rim of the eye. The nostrils are wide and open. A downturned nose is highly undesirable, as are pinched nostrils. Pigmentation of the muzzle should be as uniform as possible.

The eyes are large, round, dark and set well apart, but not prominent. They have a warm expression. Lighter-coloured eyes are permitted in liver-coloured dogs or dogs with liver markings. The whites of the eyes should not be visible.
The ears are large and pendant, with long ear leathers. They are set slightly below the crown of the skull and are so heavily coated that they appear to blend into the hair on the neck.
The mouth is wide, with a level or slightly undershot bite. The lips fit closely together.
The neck is well proportioned and gracefully arched, with sufficient length to carry the head proudly.
The shoulders are well laid back. The forelegs are short, muscular and strongly boned, as straight as possible while accommodating a broad, deep chest.

The body length from the withers to the root of the tail is greater than the height at the withers; the body is well coupled and sturdy. The chest is broad and deep. The shoulders are firm and the back is straight.

The hind legs are short, muscular and heavily boned. Viewed from behind, they should appear straight. The thighs should be well rounded and muscular. The abundant coat should give them a substantial appearance.
The feet are round and firm, with thick pads; they appear large because of the abundant hair covering them.
The tail is heavily plumed and carried gaily over the back. It is set on high. The height of the tail should be approximately level with the skull, giving the dog a balanced outline.
The coat is long and dense, not curly, with a good undercoat. A slight wave is permitted. Tying up the hair on the head is strongly recommended.
All colours are permitted. In particoloured dogs, a white blaze on the forehead and a white tip to the tail are highly desirable.

Weight ranges from 4,5 to 8,1 kg (10 - 18 pounds). The ideal weight is between 4,5 and 7,3 kg (10 - 16 pounds). Height at the withers should not exceed 26,7 cm (10,5 inches). Conformation and breed characteristics must always be of primary importance, and size alone must never be the deciding factor.
Males should have two apparently normal testicles fully descended into the scrotum.
MOVEMENT
Proud in carriage, with smooth, free-flowing movement; the forelegs reach well forward, with strong drive from the hindquarters, fully revealing the pads of the hind feet.
MAIN FAULTS
Any departure from the points above should be considered a fault, and its seriousness should be judged in proportion to the degree of deviation from the standard.
